sections.b: Moses tells the tribes to divide between two facing mountains after the crossing, six on Gerizim to bless and six on Ebal for the curse (Deuteronomy 27:11–13). The Levites then call out twelve curses on wrongs done in secret: idols, contempt for parents, moved boundary stones, misleading the blind, injustice to foreigners, orphans and widows, incest, secret killing and bribes, and finally on anyone who does not make the whole law stand. The people answer each one, "Amen" (27:14–26). Joshua carries out the ceremony (Joshua 8:30–35).

Fourteen verses of blessing (Deuteronomy 28:1–14) are followed by fifty-four of curse (28:15–68). Each blessing is reversed, then the curses grow: disease, drought, defeat, a nation from far away, siege and cannibalism, scattering, and a return to Egypt as unsold slaves. Leviticus 26 is the parallel. The closest outside match is the loyalty oath Esarhaddon of Assyria imposed in 672 BC, which has the bronze sky and iron ground and the eating of children; scholars debate whether Deuteronomy borrowed from it directly or shares an older treaty tradition.

sections.h: Life and death set before you
sections.b: The covenant ends with a choice: "life and what is good, death and what is bad" (Deuteronomy 30:15). Heaven and earth are witnesses, and Moses pleads, "Choose life" (30:19). This became a key text in debates over free will (Sirach 15:15–17; Erasmus and Luther) and in the Jewish and Christian "two ways" teaching (Didache 1:1; Matthew 7:13–14).

sections.h: Paul and the curse of the law
sections.b: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 in its Greek form, "Cursed is everyone who does not stay with all the things written in the book of the law, so as to do them" (Galatians 3:10), and 21:23 on the one hanged on a tree, to argue that Christ took the law's curse on himself (Galatians 3:13). Readers differ on whether Paul means that no individual can keep the law perfectly, or that Israel as a nation lay under the covenant curse of exile.

common: Deuteronomy 28 means God always rewards obedience with wealth and punishes sin with poverty, for every individual.
uncommon: Some scholars think Deuteronomy 28 was written as a counter-treaty: Judah swears loyalty to the LORD in place of the Assyrian king, using the Assyrian oath's own curses.

sections.b: Forty years after Sinai, Moses makes a covenant with the next generation in the land of Moab, "besides the covenant he had made with them at Horeb" (Deuteronomy 29:1). Everyone stands there, from chiefs to water carriers, with women, children and foreigners (29:10–11), and the covenant is also made "for the one who is not here with us today" (29:15). It is sealed with an alah, a curse-oath (29:12). The rabbis counted three covenants: Horeb, Moab and Ebal-Gerizim (Talmud Sotah 37b).

Ancient treaties named gods as witnesses. Israel's covenant names heaven and earth (Deuteronomy 30:19; 31:28; 32:1), a written scroll placed beside the ark (31:26), and a song the people must memorize (31:19–21). The prophets later call the same witnesses when God brings his case against Israel (Isaiah 1:2; Micah 6:1–2).

Shechem lies in the pass between Mount Ebal to the north and Mount Gerizim to the south. Deuteronomy orders the stones, the altar and the blessing-and-curse ceremony there (Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:1–26), and Joshua carries it out (Joshua 8:30–35). In the 1980s Adam Zertal excavated a stone structure on Ebal from about 1200 BC that he identified as Joshua's altar; others think it was a watchtower or farmhouse. The Samaritan Torah reads "Gerizim" for "Ebal" in Deuteronomy 27:4.

The Samaritan Pentateuch reads Mount Gerizim where the Jewish text of Deuteronomy 27:4 has Mount Ebal, adds a commandment to the Ten Commandments to build an altar on Gerizim, and says "the place the LORD has chosen" instead of "will choose" (Deuteronomy 12:5). An Old Latin witness also reads "Garzin" in 27:4, so some scholars think "Gerizim" is the original reading and "Ebal" a Jewish change. Excavations by Yitzhak Magen found a Samaritan temple city on Gerizim from the 5th or 4th century BC, destroyed by John Hyrcanus around 110 BC.

The Samaritans do not accept the Prophets as Scripture. Their hope centers on the Taheb, "the one who returns," whom they identify with the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18; 34:10; see the page on the prophet like Moses). The Samaritan woman's expectation of one who "will tell us everything" (John 4:25) fits this hope.

Deuteronomy 27:2–8 commands large stones, coated with lime plaster and inscribed with "all the words of this law," to be set up after the crossing, beside an altar of uncut stones. Writing on plaster was a known way to display a public text; the Balaam inscription from Deir Alla was painted on a plastered wall. The Mishnah says the words were written in seventy languages (Mishnah Sotah 7:5).

sections.h: Writing, keeping and reading the law
sections.b: Deuteronomy 31 tells how Moses wrote "this law" in a scroll, gave it to the Levites and elders, had it placed beside the ark, and ordered it read to all the people every seventh year at the Feast of Booths (Deuteronomy 31:9–13, 24–26). From "write down this song for yourselves" (31:19) the rabbis derived the last commandment in the Torah's order (number 613 in Sefer HaChinukh; positive 18 for Maimonides): each Jew must write a Torah scroll (Talmud Sanhedrin 21b). The first verse a Jewish child learned was "Moses commanded us a law, the heritage of the assembly of Jacob" (33:4; Talmud Sukkah 42a).

Deuteronomy 34 describes Moses' death and says no one knows his grave "to this day." The Talmud records two views: Joshua wrote the last eight verses, or Moses wrote them in tears at God's dictation (Bava Batra 15a; Menachot 30a). Ibn Ezra held that Joshua wrote from 34:1 on, and Spinoza used these verses to argue that Moses did not write the Torah.

The curses of Deuteronomy 28 end in exile: a king led away (28:36), scattering "from one end of the earth to the other" (28:64), no rest for the sole of the foot (28:65), and a return to Egypt (28:68). Chapter 29 imagines the nations asking why the land is ruined, and Israel uprooted and flung "into another land, where they are today" (29:28). Ramban read Leviticus 26 as the Babylonian exile and Deuteronomy 28 as the longer exile after Rome.

Deuteronomy 30:1–10 promises that Israel, scattered among the nations, will take the words to heart and return, and the LORD will turn back their captivity and gather them "even from the farthest edge of the sky." Nehemiah prays this promise (Nehemiah 1:8–9), and Maimonides held that the Torah guarantees Israel's repentance and redemption (Laws of Repentance 7:5).

The Hebrew verb shuv, "turn, return," occurs seven times in Deuteronomy 30:1–10: Israel turns back to the LORD, and the LORD turns back Israel's captivity and turns again to rejoice over it. The Talmud notes that the verb says God himself "will return," so his presence shares Israel's exile (Megillah 29a). The chapter is read before the Jewish New Year, in the season of teshuvah.

In Deuteronomy 10:16 Israel is told to circumcise its own heart; in 30:6 God promises to do it, "so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and all your being." The promise grows into the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26. Paul speaks of circumcision "of the heart, in spirit and not in letter" (Romans 2:29), and Ramban read the verse as the messianic age, when doing good becomes second nature.

sections.h: The nations and the sons of God
sections.b: In the oldest Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 32:8, a Dead Sea Scroll, the Most High fixes the nations' borders "by the number of the sons of God," while the LORD keeps Jacob as his own share (32:9). The Greek has "angels of God" and the Masoretic "sons of Israel." With Deuteronomy 4:19 and 29:26, the verse pictures other nations given over to heavenly beings or to the sun, moon and stars, while Israel belongs to the LORD directly. Jewish tradition spoke of seventy angels over seventy nations (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan; compare Daniel 10:13, 20). In the scroll's form of 32:43, the Song ends by calling "all you gods" to bow down to the LORD.

common: The "sons of God" in Deuteronomy 32:8 are simply the people of Israel, as the King James Version reads.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Most High (Elyon) of Deuteronomy 32:8 was once a different god from the LORD, who received Israel as his share.

sections.b: The Song of Moses mocks gods that are "not God" (Deuteronomy 32:17, 21) and climaxes with God's words: "I, only I, am he; there is no god alongside me" (32:39). Yet the same Song speaks of "sons of God" over the nations (32:8) and, in its oldest form, calls "all you gods" to bow down (32:43). Scholars debate whether this shows an older belief in many divine beings under one supreme God, or a monotheism that denies other gods any real power. Isaiah 43:10–13 takes up the Song's "I am he."

God tells Moses to write a song and teach it, so that it will testify against Israel when disaster comes (Deuteronomy 31:19–22). The Song (32:1–43) calls heaven and earth to listen, praises God the Rock, recalls how he found Jacob in the desert and carried him like an eagle, accuses Jeshurun of growing fat and turning to demons, and announces judgment. Then it turns: God will not let the enemy boast, vengeance belongs to him, and he will rescue his people and make atonement for the land. Scholars call it a covenant "lawsuit"; proposed dates range from the 11th century BC to the exile.

sections.h: The Song in the New Testament
sections.b: Few Old Testament passages are quoted as often. Paul uses 32:21 for Israel's jealousy of the Gentiles (Romans 10:19), 32:35 for leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19), 32:43 for Gentiles rejoicing with Israel (Romans 15:10), and 32:17 for sacrifices to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20). Hebrews quotes 32:43 in its Greek form, "Let all God's angels worship him" (Hebrews 1:6), and 32:35–36 (Hebrews 10:30). Revelation 15:3 has the victors sing "the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb."
sections.refs: Romans 10:19; Romans 12:19; Romans 15:10; 1 Corinthians 10:20; Hebrews 1:6; Hebrews 10:30; Revelation 15:3

sections.b: The Dead Sea Scrolls changed the study of the Song of Moses. 4QDeut-j reads "sons of God" in Deuteronomy 32:8, where the Masoretic Text has "sons of Israel," and 4QDeut-q gives 32:43 a longer form, with "all you gods, bow down to him," that the Septuagint also knew and Hebrews 1:6 quotes. Most textual critics think the scrolls keep the older wording and that later scribes softened language about other heavenly beings. Other famous differences in Deuteronomy 27–34 include Ebal or Gerizim (27:4) and "Give Levi your Thummim" (33:8).

"Rock" (tsur) is the Song of Moses' main name for God: "He is the Rock; what he does is flawless" (Deuteronomy 32:4; also 32:15, 18, 30–31). The Greek translators usually rendered it "God." Psalms and Isaiah take up the title (Psalm 18:2; Isaiah 44:8), and Paul says the rock that followed Israel in the wilderness "was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Deuteronomy 33:26 gives God the old storm god's title, the one who rides the clouds.

sections.b: God tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo, see the land and die, because of his unfaithfulness at Meribah (Deuteronomy 32:48–52). Moses blesses the tribes (chapter 33), sees the whole land, and dies "at the LORD's word" at 120, his eyes still sharp; God buries him and no one knows the grave (34:1–7). The rabbis said he died by God's kiss (Bava Batra 17a) and drew from his burial the duty to bury the dead (Sotah 14a). Josephus says Moses wrote of his own death so that no one would claim he had been taken up to God (Antiquities 4.326). Jude 9 knows a story of Michael disputing with the devil over his body.

The Torah ends: "No prophet has risen again in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face" (Deuteronomy 34:10), and recalls the signs in Egypt and the great deeds done before all Israel (34:11–12). Moses is remembered not as a king or conqueror but as the one who knew God most closely. On how the epitaph relates to the promise of "a prophet like me" (18:15), see the page on the prophet like Moses.

claude.title: The grave no one could find
claude.body: My suggestion: the unknown grave (Deuteronomy 34:6) completes a pattern in Deuteronomy, which repeatedly forbids honoring the dead or holy places outside the one chosen place (12:2–5; 14:1; 18:11). A tomb of Moses would have become the obvious rival shrine. Hiding it keeps Israel's loyalty on the word Moses left (31:24–26) rather than on the man. This overlaps with a common Jewish and Christian explanation, but I would stress that the burial notice reads as part of Deuteronomy's larger program against localized cults of the dead.

sections.b: Moses tells the people that Joshua will cross at their head, then charges Joshua before all Israel: "Be strong and bold," for the LORD "will not let you down, and he will not abandon you" (Deuteronomy 31:3–8). The LORD himself commissions Joshua at the tent of meeting (31:14–15, 23). After Moses' death Joshua is "filled with a spirit of wisdom" because Moses had laid his hands on him, and the people listen to him (34:9). Joshua 1 repeats the charge four times.

Before his death Moses blesses the tribes (Deuteronomy 33), as Jacob blessed his sons (Genesis 49). Reuben may live though his men be few; Judah is helped against his foes; Levi receives the Urim and Thummim and the duty to teach; Benjamin rests near God; Joseph's land is rich and his horns are a wild ox's; Zebulun and Issachar draw wealth from the seas; Gad is a lion and Dan a lion's cub; Naphtali is full of favor; Asher dips his foot in oil. Simeon is missing, perhaps because it had been absorbed into Judah (Joshua 19:1–9). Six tribes stand on Gerizim and six on Ebal for the covenant ceremony (27:12–13).

In Moses' blessing, Levi's first gift is the priest's lots: "Give Levi your Thummim, and your Urim to your loyal one" (Deuteronomy 33:8, following a Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek; the Masoretic Text lacks "Give Levi"). It is the only place where Thummim is named first. Levi earns them by loyalty at Massah and Meribah and at the golden calf (33:8–9; Exodus 32:26–29).

God tells Moses that when Israel turns to other gods, "I will abandon them and hide my face from them" (Deuteronomy 31:17–18; 32:20). Hester panim, the hiding of the face, became a Jewish way to speak of times when God seems absent. The Talmud found Esther, the book where God is never named, hinted in the word "I will hide" (Chullin 139b). After the Holocaust, Martin Buber wrote of an "eclipse of God," and Eliezer Berkovits argued that God hides so that human freedom can be real.

"What is hidden is for the LORD our God. What has been made known is for us and our children for all time, so that we will carry out every word of this law" (Deuteronomy 29:29). The verse sets limits on human knowledge and points to what God has made plain; Calvin used it against speculation about predestination.

Every seventh year, in the Year of Release, all Israel was to gather at the Feast of Booths to hear the law read aloud: men, women, children and foreigners (Deuteronomy 31:10–13). The Mishnah describes the king reading Deuteronomy in the temple court, and King Agrippa weeping at the law against a foreign king (Mishnah Sotah 7:8). Nehemiah 8 records a great reading at Booths after the exile.

From Mount Nebo the LORD shows Moses the whole land, from Gilead and Dan to the western sea and the Negev, and says: "This is the land I swore to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob ... I have let you see it for yourself, but you will not go over there" (Deuteronomy 34:1–4). The five books of Moses end with the promise still ahead. Hebrews reads the ending as a sign that the true homeland is still to come (Hebrews 11:13–16).

sections.h: The word is close by you
sections.b: Moses says God's command is not "in the sky" or "on the far side of the sea": "The word is close by you, very close: in your mouth and in your heart, for you to do" (Deuteronomy 30:11–14). In the Talmud, Rabbi Joshua answers a heavenly voice with "It is not in heaven," meaning the Torah is now for humans to interpret (Bava Metzia 59b). Paul applies the passage to Christ and "the word of faith" (Romans 10:6–8). Moses also says of the law, "this is not an empty word for you. It is your life" (32:47).

The Song of Moses pictures God like an eagle that stirs its nest, hovers over its young, and carries them on its feathers (Deuteronomy 32:11). The verb "hovers" is the one used of God's Spirit over the waters in Genesis 1:2. Exodus 19:4 uses the same image of the exodus. In Deuteronomy 27:20 the "wing" of a cloak stands for a marriage claim, as in Ruth 3:9.

Deuteronomy 18:15 promises "a prophet like me," but the Torah closes by saying that no prophet like Moses had arisen, one whom the LORD knew face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10). The verse may look back from a time when prophets had come and none had matched him. Jews have held that none ever will equal him: Maimonides made the unique rank of Moses' prophecy the seventh of his principles of faith. Christians read the promise as fulfilled in Jesus, who like Moses speaks God's words and leads a new exodus (Acts 3:22–23; John 6:14; Hebrews 3:1–6). Samaritans await the Taheb, a prophet like Moses.

sections.h: A prophet, not only a king
sections.b: Not every hope for a coming deliverer looked for a king. The closing verses of Deuteronomy, which say no prophet had yet arisen like Moses (Deuteronomy 34:10), fed the expectation of a coming Prophet alongside an anointed king (John 1:21; John 6:14). See the page on the prophet like Moses.

In the Song of Moses God says, "Vengeance belongs to me, and payback, for the time their foot slips" (Deuteronomy 32:35). Here vengeance means the just ruler setting things right, turned against Israel's enemies once Israel is helpless (32:36–43). Paul quotes it to tell believers not to avenge themselves (Romans 12:19); Hebrews uses it as a warning (Hebrews 10:30); Jonathan Edwards preached "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741) on the slipping foot. The rabbis read 28:63 so that God does not rejoice when people perish (Megillah 10b).

The Song of Moses says God "came upon" Israel "in a wilderness land, in a waste where the wild winds howl," and guarded him like the pupil of his eye (Deuteronomy 32:10). The Song does not mention Egypt; like Hosea 9:10 and Jeremiah 2:2, it remembers the desert as the place where God and Israel first belonged to each other. In 29:5 Moses recalls forty years in which clothes and sandals did not wear out.
